analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal income tax and replaces it with a 15 percent national sales tax, abolishing the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in May 1999 with 21 cosponsors, it got no markup, no vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and several excise taxes, and impose a 15 percent tax on everything consumers buy in the United States. Business purchases and exports would be exempt, states that conform their own sales taxes would collect the federal tax for a 1 percent fee, the IRS would be phased out after 2003, and every family would receive a rebate covering the tax on spending up to the federal poverty level. Raising the rate would require a supermajority in the House and Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and wealthy households gain the most: with the income, capital gains, and estate taxes repealed, their federal tax bill on earnings and inherited wealth drops to zero, and the sales tax falls only on what they spend. Tax filers at every income level escape annual filing and audit exposure. Retailers and the conforming states get paid to run the new tax: retailers receive an administrative credit of the greater of $200 or half a percent of tax remitted, and states keep a 1 percent collection fee.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, estate and gift taxes, and several excise taxes, ending annual income tax filing for individuals and businesses.
Imposes a 15 percent tax on goods and services purchased for personal use, with exemptions for business inputs and exports.
Gives each family a 'family consumption refund' paid through paychecks, equal to the tax on spending up to the federal poverty level for their household size.
Exempts tuition for primary, secondary, and university education and job-related training from the tax.
Lets states that adopt a conforming sales tax collect the federal tax and keep a 1 percent administration fee, and prohibits any IRS appropriations after fiscal year 2003.
Requires a supermajority in both the House and Senate to raise the tax rate.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers bear the new 15 percent tax on everything they buy. Because families with low and middle incomes spend nearly all of their income while high earners spend only a fraction of theirs, the tax takes a much larger share of a working family's budget, and the rebate offsets the tax only on spending up to the poverty line. State and local governments and nonprofits would also owe the tax on their own purchases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers who spend most of their income

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to all consumption but the rebate covers only spending up to the poverty level, so a family earning modestly above poverty pays the full 15 percent on every additional dollar spent while wealthy households pay it on only a small slice of their income, making the overall system lighter at the top and heavier in the middle and bottom.
Repealing the estate and gift taxes and the income tax on capital gains delivers the largest dollar benefit to the wealthiest households, funded by the new consumption tax everyone pays.

The stated 15 percent rate is charged on payments that already include the tax, so the effective markup at the register is about 17.6 percent, and it stacks on top of the state sales taxes states would keep or conform.
Federal, state, and local governments and qualified nonprofits must pay the tax on their own purchases, raising the cost of public services.
Businesses still face monthly tax reports, registration, penalties, and criminal exposure for willful failures, so the compliance burden shifts from individuals to sellers rather than disappearing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending income tax filing would be a real, tangible relief for tens of millions of households, and the poverty-level rebate shields the poorest families from the new tax. But the trade is a bad one for most working people: taxing consumption instead of income shifts the total burden down the income ladder, and the biggest giveaways (no estate tax, no capital gains tax) go to those at the top. The transition also carries serious revenue and enforcement risks, since a state-run collection system replacing the IRS was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee (and the Rules Committee) the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Billy Tauzin introduced the National Retail Sales Tax Act of 1999 on May 27, 1999, with 18 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee for consideration.
A total of 21 members cosponsored the bill: 18 Republicans and 3 Democrats.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress, and died on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax structure and the interests it favors were better off: high-income households kept untaxed capital gains and estate transfers, and the tax preparation and compliance industry kept its market. Working families also avoided a consumption tax that would have taken a larger share of their income, but the filing relief and rebate they were promised never arrived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households and the tax-prep industry

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican, with 18 of the 21 cosponsors Republicans and only 3 Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a floor vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.note: Repeal of the income, capital gains, and estate and gift taxes would eliminate federal tax on the largest concentrations of private wealth, with the lost revenue replaced by a consumption tax paid by everyone. The benefit scales with wealth while the cost scales with spending.

Retailers would take on the job of collecting and remitting a 15 percent federal tax on every sale, with penalties for failure, but would be paid an administrative credit of the greater of $200 or 0.5 percent of tax remitted plus a 50 percent credit for compliance equipment. The cost of collection would largely be passed into prices.

States that conform their sales taxes to the federal design become the permanent collection arm for the national tax, keeping a 1 percent administration fee. This locks state governments into a federal revenue role in exchange for funding.

The bill taxes brokerage, banking, insurance, and fund fees, plus an imputed tax on interest spreads, but exempts the first $10,000 of such payments per year and gives firms bad-debt credits. The tax would be passed on to account holders and borrowers through fees and rates.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax compliance industry
industries.note: Abolishing the income tax and the IRS eliminates the annual filing and audit system the industry is built on. Its loss mirrors the relief individual taxpayers would gain from no longer filing.
